name: roles
description: The roles an admin creates on top of the default ones. The default roles are not in here and never will be: they are defined in code, their rights are in ../rights.json, and this table cannot overwrite either.

columns.name: id
columns.description: Referenced by role_rights.role_id. Not by user_roles, which links by name — see there.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Unique, and what user_roles.role holds. Must not equal a RoleNames value: a created role that shadows a default one would be unreachable, because the default is resolved first. The database cannot check that — the code enum is not visible to it — so the application rejects it on write and a contract test asserts the check exists.

columns.name: parent_role
columns.description: The default role this role starts from, as a RoleNames value. A name and not a foreign key because there is no row to point at, and because only a default role may be inherited from — which a varchar checked against the code enum says exactly, with no cycles to detect. NULL means an empty base: every right has to be granted explicitly.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Written on every change to the role AND on every insert, update or delete in role_rights for it, in the same transaction. MAX(updated_at) over this table lets an instance skip a rebuild it does not need; it is not what bounds staleness — the cache TTL is.

columns.name: updated_by_user_id
columns.description: The admin who made the change. NULL for anything written outside the application.

notes: Nothing seeds this table. An instance that never creates a role has an empty one, and every account still has its rights — they come from the default roles in code.
The rights of a row are the rows in role_rights, applied to the default set of parent_role. A row with no role_rights rows is exactly its parent role under a different name.

Renaming a role rewrites user_roles.role for every holder in the same transaction, because that column holds the name. It is a handful of rows and one statement; what is not allowed is renaming without it, which would leave holders pointing at a name nothing answers to.

Deleting a role is blocked while user_roles still references its name. The admin frontend reassigns first — there is no cascade, because losing rights silently is not something a foreign key should be allowed to decide.

Cached process-globally with the 10 minute TTL Architecture.md sets for role rights, and invalidated immediately when an admin edits a role on that instance. Another instance sees the change within the TTL. That bound is the answer, not a poll interval — the same rule applies to settings.
Not scoped by community, for the reason db/settings.json gives: an instance has exactly one home community, and a foreign community's roles are not this instance's business.
Tens of rows, read whole into the cache. No index beyond the primary key and the unique name.
Timestamps are UTC milliseconds; see types/Timestamp.json.
Identifiers are uint64 throughout; see contracts/AGENTS.md.

A created role is assignable: role.assign takes the name as text and resolves it as db/user_roles.json describes. The route it replaces typed that field as the RoleNames enum, which is why this table was writable only by hand until now.
